title: Backups, phrases and output
goal: How the generator adds a joined (+) way into every word beside its primary, merges two words into one stroke, and writes the dictionary files out.

blocks.x: Backup composition: every + way into a word

Once every primary is locked in, a fixed-point pass builds `+`-joined entries for every word it can. Each is reached by sounding a word out from pieces you already know: a placed stem, an ending, a prefix, or the word's own syllables. A rare word can keep a terse one-stroke primary ([[machete|PHEFPT]]) and still be typed from its sound ([[PHU/+SHE/+TAOE]]).

items: There are about 205,400 backups in the current build.
They are placed before the bonus short forms.
A phrase never takes a backup of more than one stroke.
No backup can change a primary.
A word may have several. When two words compose the same text in one round, the more frequently said word wins it.

blocks.x: What every direction builds on

items: A placed word's **fastest outline**, and also its own plain reading when that is a longer form.
Any `+*` ladder marker on the stem is dropped, so no join has a star in the middle of it.
A join of three strokes or more whose last stroke fits on the one before (right-hand keys, all later in steno order) is offered folded too.
A word's "best" outline, which later rounds use as a stem, is picked by strokes, then keys, then ergonomics, then the outline text itself, so the choice never depends on entry order.
Joins through an ending build on the stem's plain reading, never its brief. The stem is three letters or more, the join must pass the fragment check, and a word in `-ly` never joins through `-y`.
Every round's compositions are collected on every core, up to five rounds.

blocks.x: The directions

head: Direction
Mechanic
rows: A placed stem's outline plus a reduced trailing syllable as one joined stroke (build + -ing).
A stem found by spelling plus a known two-stroke suffix (`-ism`, `-ary`, `-ical`, ...).
OR a leading consonant cluster into a placed stem's first stroke, when the keys are disjoint. No stroke is added; the stem's later strokes are carried through untouched.

A family member's stem outline, whatever it is, plus the ending's standalone stroke: call + -ed is [[KAUL/+-D]], look + -s is [[HRAOBG/+-S]]. Covers endings that are not a syllable of their own, which (a) cannot.

The word itself, one syllable per stroke, from each pronunciation: its folded outline; a reduced last syllable struck like a suffix ([[TAEU/+-BL]]); every vowel written ([[TAEU/+PWUL]]); both syllable splits ([[HREPL/+UPB]], [[HRE/+PHUPB]]); a fixed prefix folded or alone. A kept schwa is always `U`. Needs no other word, so it runs in round 0 only.
A prefix's own stroke, then the placed stem's whole outline joined: [[UPB/+KHRAOER]] (unclear), [[TKE/+KOED]] (decode), [[TPHOPB/+STOP]] (nonstop). The word's sound must end in the stem's.
Two placed words back to back, when the spelling really is the two words joined (myself = my + self).
The same, found by letters and a loose consonant check, for pairs CMUdict does not split cleanly: [[PHO/+WUPB]] (noone = no + one). See [syllables and folding](#/ref/syllables).

blocks.x: Direction (f) uses eighteen prefixes: un, dis, mis, re, pre, de, co, en, im, in, non, sub, trans, anti, inter, semi, over, under. See [prefixes](#/ref/prefixes).
Endings used by direction (d)

head: List
Endings
rows: Family endings (also shape a family's primary)
Extra backup-only endings (never move a primary)
`-ation -ist -ish -ism -ize -ous -ive -ic -al -age -ity -ward -en -y -or -ible`, e.g. art + -ist is [[ART/+EUFT]] and sail + -or is [[SAEUL/+-R]]
`-or` is written with `-er`'s stroke and `-ible` with `-able`'s

blocks.x: Longest ending first, so information is inform + -ation, never a non-word + -on. An ending that replaces part of the stem (`-tion`, `-ic`, `-ity`) is reached by the sound-based directions (a), (e), not by a spelling-based family link.
How many joined ways in
Every word of two syllables or more has joined ways in, however terse its primary is. See [every way to join a word](#/ref/ways-to-join).
Phrase-briefing: two words in one stroke

When two words' primaries share no keys, their union is a stroke nobody has claimed. "of" is `-F` and "the" is `-T`; their OR is [[-FT]], a brand-new stroke that writes both. "of the" is the commonest bigram in the corpus (2,766,332,391 occurrences). Phrases are written on the page [phrase-briefing](#/ref/phrases); this section is the build mechanism.

head: Step
Rule
rows: The 20,000 most frequent bigrams, ranked by raw bigram count (not a collocation score: "of the" and "in the" are the most worth briefing because both halves are independently common).
Disjoint-OR of the two words' primaries.

One side may be a multi-stroke word. The single-stroke side merges into the other's **first** stroke only, by the same disjoint-OR rule as backup direction (b), and the rest of the host is carried through untouched: a (`A`) + currency (`KURPB/+SEU`) is `KAURPB/+SEU`.

A bigram's lowercase "i" is looked up as the "I" entry on [[EU]], so phrases build on the pronoun, not the letter. `EU` shares vowel keys with most verbs, so few "I" phrases qualify; "I would" is [[WOEU]].

blocks.x: Who gives up a stroke
A pair whose merged stroke a word already holds competes for it on count. Three limits apply:

head: Limit
Value
rows: the 5,000 most frequent (a phrase may still take one of their short forms or alternates)
Pairs allowed to take a held stroke at all
only the 1,000 most frequent eligible pairs; a rarer pair is committed only into a free stroke

blocks.x: With these limits 134 words carry a star because a phrase took their stroke, 15 of them in the top 5,000. The build has 5,720 phrase entries.
The phrasing grammar

The phrasing grammar writes a whole phrase in one stroke by rule: a starter (who) on the left bank, the auxiliary or tense on the vowels, the star for not, and a verb on the right bank. Learn it in [the lessons](#/lesson/19-phrasing-grammar) and drill the strokes in [the phrasing strokes lesson](#/lesson/20-phrasing-strokes).
Output: writing the dictionary files

Inside the generator every word is keyed lowercase. `write_json` applies one transform on the way out, `written()`: the pronoun "i", alone, leading a contraction, or as either half of a phrase, is capitalized.

head: Stroke
Written as
rows: eye (the letter i is not given this stroke)

blocks.x: A full `!build` takes about 8 seconds. `score --check-readme` takes about 4.6 seconds; `--write-readme` rewrites stale README tables.
Checks that run on every build and test run

items: No two raw entries share an outline. `write_json` keys by outline text, so a duplicate would silently lose an entry.
A word's cheapest outline does not depend on entry order.
The top 1,000 words are one stroke each, with no `/+*` ladder marker. Only american and lt, which have no one-stroke candidate at all, are exempt.
The solver matches brute force on 300 random over-subscribed graphs.
No word is stranded on a worse outline than one of its own unclaimed candidates, and every word in the top 2,000 has an outline.
A reduced "-er" keeps its R, and a sound may only explain a key on a stroke it can actually be on (each pinned by a test).
